mcqs.question: A system is roughly 100:1 read-heavy. Which toolkit best matches that workload?
options: Sharding writes across many nodes and buffering incoming data
Read replicas and aggressive caching, since the goal is serving the same data to many readers cheaply
A single large database instance with no replicas, since reads never need to scale
Synchronous multi-region writes to guarantee every reader sees the latest data instantly
mcqs.explanation: Read-heavy systems get the most leverage from spreading read load across replicas and caching hot data, since the same data is served to many readers. Sharded writes and buffering solve a write-volume problem this system doesn't have, and a single unreplicated instance would struggle under exactly the read load described.

mcqs.question: Adding many indexes to speed up reads has what effect on the write path?
options: Each write now has to update every index too, slowing writes down
Indexes have no effect on writes, only on reads
Indexes speed up both reads and writes equally
Indexes only affect storage size, never latency
mcqs.explanation: Every index needs to be kept in sync with the underlying data, so each additional index adds work to every write that touches it — read optimization isn't free on the write side. Indexes clearly aren't write-neutral, don't speed up writes, and affect latency, not just storage.

mcqs.question: A system's read:write ratio is roughly 50:50. What's the strongest way to decide where to invest optimization effort?
options: Always default to the read-heavy toolkit, since reads are slightly more common in most real systems
Optimization doesn't matter at all once the ratio is balanced
Look at the cost asymmetry — whether a slow read or a slow write is more visible or costly — and let that guide the design instead of the raw ratio
Flip a coin between the read-heavy and write-heavy toolkits
mcqs.explanation: When the ratio itself doesn't clearly favor one side, the more useful signal is which failure mode actually costs more — a laggy user-facing read is often more visible than a delayed background write, for instance. Defaulting to one toolkit or leaving it to chance ignores information you can actually gather.

mcqs.question: A metrics ingestion pipeline with heavy write volume and rare reads gets a new read cache added because "caching is always good." What's the issue?
options: There is no issue — caching always improves any system's performance
The cache should have been added to the write path instead of the read path
Caching is inherently insecure and should never be used in production systems
A cache only helps when the same data is read repeatedly — here it adds complexity and invalidation overhead for little benefit while ignoring the real write bottleneck
mcqs.explanation: Caching pays off when reads repeat over the same data; a write-heavy pipeline with rare reads has little repeated read traffic to benefit from, so the cache is mostly added cost without addressing the write bottleneck that actually matters here. Caches aren't inherently a write-path concept or a security risk.
